HotLoop Edge first shipped in 4.18.10. The image is `ghcr.io/hotloop-io/hotloop-edge:4.18.10`, built for amd64, arm64 and arm/v7, and the chart is `hotloop-edge` in the same Helm repository as the rest of the lineup. Both pull with no login. There is no Docker or Compose path, on purpose, and a bare `podman run` from a shell that dies with the session isn't an install.

A cluster gets Helm. An industrial PC or a Pi with no cluster gets Podman Quadlet. The database is a choice you make once: TimescaleDB (the default), plain PostgreSQL, or a SQLite file with no database container at all.

## Helm

```bash
helm repo add hotloop https://hotloop.io/hotloop
helm repo update
helm install hotloop hotloop/hotloop-edge --version 4.18.10 \
  --namespace hotloop --create-namespace
```

Call the release `hotloop` whichever product it is. The release name is what the database's volume, the Secrets and the Service are named after, and keeping it is what lets a site move up a product later.

That deploys Edge plus TimescaleDB 2.30.1 beside it on a 20 Gi volume, keeping 90 days of history. The chart generates the database password, the MCP token and an admin password into the release Secret, and reuses them on every upgrade. It generates `<release>-secret-key` too, the key that encrypts every device password HotLoop keeps. That key is part of your data, and [the Gateway install page](/gateway/install/#back-up-the-key-before-you-need-it) says why and how to back it up. It is the same key.

For plain PostgreSQL or a SQLite file, set `database.type` to `postgresql` or `sqlite` when you install. A SQLite file is one writer on one local disk, so it is one replica and never NFS. Moving between databases later is a backup and a restore, because the new database starts empty. [Backups](/iot/backup/) has the restore.

### Sign in

The user is `admin`. The install notes print the command that reads the password back:

```bash
kubectl -n hotloop get secret hotloop \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.admin-password}' | base64 -d
kubectl -n hotloop port-forward svc/hotloop 8080:8080
```

Open `http://localhost:8080`. Writes ship off: every tag is read-only until somebody arms it, and `safety.allowWrites` stays `false` until you decide this box gets to move machinery. [The write gate](/gateway/write-gate/) has every check, in order.

### What Edge adds, and how to turn it on

Both are off by default, because opening a listener or an uplink on a plant network is something a deployment does on purpose.

**The OPC UA server** is `opcuaServer.enabled: true`, on port 4840. Set `opcuaServer.endpointHost` to the name a client reaches the box at, so the certificate matches it. [The OPC UA server](/edge/opc-ua-server/) has the security model, and it is read-only.

**Sparkplug publishing** is `edgePublish.enabled: true`, with `edgePublish.broker` and `edgePublish.group` required. Set `edgePublish.node` too, or the node id is the release name. The forward queue lives on a 1 Gi volume, `edgePublish.queueMaxBytes` defaults to 64 MiB (about two and three quarter minutes at 2,000 readings a second, at about 180 bytes a reading), and past it the oldest readings are dropped and counted. `0` is unbounded, and a long enough outage then fills the volume. Edge publishing needs `replicaCount` 1, and the chart refuses to render otherwise. [Edge publish and store-and-forward](/edge/edge-publish/) has what it does when the uplink dies.

### What to set before a real plant sees it

| Value | Default | Why you'd touch it |
|---|---|---|
| `plant.name`, `plant.siteId` | `HotLoop`, empty | What the plant is called on screens, in pages, and to other sites. |
| `global.timezone` | `America/New_York` | Schedules and shift changes run on it. It has to be a real zone name. |
| `publicUrl` | empty | The address a phone on the plant Wi-Fi reaches HotLoop at. Without it, notifications have no link back. |
| `safety.allowWrites` | `false` | The master switch. Off, nothing writes to a machine, from anywhere. |
| `historian.retentionDays` | `90` | Days of history kept. |
| `database.postgresql.persistence.size` | `20Gi` | Your history lives here. Size it for your tag count and the retention above. |
| `opcuaClient.persistence.enabled` | `false` | Turn it on before you add a secured OPC UA device, so the client's certificates survive a restart. |
| `secretKey.existingSecret` | empty | A Secret you manage holding the device password key. Set it if you render the chart with `helm template`. |

## Podman Quadlet

Quadlet turns the containers into real systemd services: they start on boot with nobody logged in, restart when they die, and log to the journal. It needs **Podman 5.0 or newer**. Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm ships 4.3, which has no Quadlet at all, so a Pi wants Trixie or newer. Put the database volume on a USB SSD and not the SD card.

The units are in the `edge/` directory of the HotLoop repository, under `deploy/quadlet/`, and they have the same names as IoT's and the Gateway's. [Podman Quadlet](/install/quadlet/) explains each file.

```bash
sudo cp hotloop.network hotloop.container hotloop-db.container \
  hotloop-db.volume hotloop-data.volume /etc/containers/systemd/

openssl rand -hex 24 | sudo podman secret create hotloop-db-password -
sudo podman run --rm ghcr.io/hotloop-io/hotloop-edge:stable gen-secret-key \
  | sudo podman secret create hotloop-secret-key -
printf '%s' 'a long admin password' \
  | sudo podman run --rm -i ghcr.io/hotloop-io/hotloop-edge:stable hash-password \
  | sudo podman secret create hotloop-admin-password-hash -

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start hotloop.service
sudo systemctl status hotloop.service hotloop-db.service
curl -s localhost:8080/api/status
```

Then open `http://<this box>:8080` and log in as `admin`. Keep a copy of the key somewhere that isn't this box, because losing it means typing every device password in again.

The unit publishes only port 8080. When you switch the OPC UA server (4840) or the embedded MQTT broker (1883) on, add a `PublishPort=` line for it to `hotloop.container`. The Quadlet unit keeps 90 days of history by default, the same as the chart.

Want plain PostgreSQL on Edge? It is the TimescaleDB unit with `Environment=HOTLOOP_HISTORIAN_TIMESCALE=false` added to `hotloop.container`. Want a SQLite file? Use the files in `edge/sqlite/` and nothing from the directory above, because they share unit names: it is `hotloop.container` and `hotloop-data.volume`, and two secrets, `hotloop-secret-key` and `hotloop-admin-password-hash`.

The unit follows `:stable`, and Podman moves it once the timer is on:

```bash
sudo systemctl enable --now podman-auto-update.timer
```

A new image migrates the database on its way up, and if it can't start, Podman puts the previous one back. The database container does not follow `:stable`, on purpose. [The :stable auto-update](/install/auto-update/) says what an update does, what a rollback cannot undo, and how to hold updates until you say. Take a backup before you turn updates on.

## Moving up a product

IoT to Edge to the Gateway keeps every device, tag, entity, automation, alarm, user and hour of history. On Quadlet it is copying the bigger product's `hotloop.container` and `hotloop-db.container` over yours, and [the lineup](/products/) has the Helm form. The Quadlet move has been run, IoT then Edge then the Gateway on one database volume. The same move as a `helm upgrade` on a real cluster, and going back down a product, have not been run, so don't take a box you care about down a product.

## What has and hasn't been run

The Edge Quadlet units are generated from the Gateway's, which were run for real, rootless under systemd, including an update that migrates and then can't start and gets rolled back. The Edge units themselves were compared to the Gateway's, not started under systemd on their own. A real Pi under systemd as root, and the 32-bit arm images on real hardware, haven't been done yet. This page will say so when they are.
